reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents with intensely itchy, grouped (herpetiform) vesicles and papules symmetrically distributed over the extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp
The itch and burning are often so severe that intact blisters are rarely seen, replaced by excoriations and crusts from scratching
It is the cutaneous expression of gluten sensitivity and is strongly associated with coeliac disease, although many patients have few or no bowel symptoms
Diagnosis rests on skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence, which shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae of perilesional skin
Supportive serology includes anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies, reflecting the shared autoimmunity with coeliac disease
A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the cornerstone of management and addresses both the skin and the associated enteropathy
A sulphone-class agent can rapidly control itch and blistering while the diet takes effect, but requires screening for enzyme deficiency and monitoring for haemolysis
Screen for associated conditions including autoimmune thyroid disease and be aware of a small increased long-term risk of small-bowel lymphoma, which dietary control reduces
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering disease driven by gluten sensitivity in genetically predisposed individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Dietary gluten triggers production of IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase and, in the skin, cross-reactivity with epidermal transglutaminase. IgA immune complexes deposit in the dermal papillae, recruiting neutrophils that form the characteristic papillary microabscesses and cause subepidermal separation with vesicle formation. The same gluten-driven autoimmunity produces the small-bowel villous atrophy of coeliac disease, so skin and gut manifestations share a common mechanism and both respond to gluten withdrawal.
additionalDifferentials: Scabies (intensely itchy, but with burrows and different distribution)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence showing granular papillary IgA (the diagnostic standard)
Coeliac serology including anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial IgA antibodies
Total IgA level to interpret serology correctly
Consideration of small-bowel evaluation in conjunction with gastroenterology
Screening for enzyme deficiency before starting sulphone therapy and for associated autoimmune disease, such as thyroid function
redFlags: New abdominal symptoms, weight loss, or anaemia raising concern for complications of coeliac disease including small-bowel lymphoma
Signs of haemolysis or methaemoglobinaemia in a patient on sulphone therapy
Widespread blistering with systemic upset prompting reconsideration of an alternative autoimmune bullous disease
Features of malabsorption or nutritional deficiency requiring investigation
reference.prognosis: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic condition, but a strict gluten-free diet usually controls the skin disease, allows medication to be reduced or stopped over time, heals the associated enteropathy, and lowers the long-term lymphoma risk; lapses in the diet typically provoke relapse.
pitfalls: Taking the biopsy for immunofluorescence from lesional rather than perilesional skin and obtaining a false-negative result
Relying on the diet alone while overlooking the need to screen for and manage associated coeliac and autoimmune disease
Starting sulphone therapy without checking for enzyme deficiency and monitoring blood counts
Attributing the intense itch to eczema or scabies and missing the diagnosis
management: Institute a strict lifelong gluten-free diet as the cornerstone, treating both the skin disease and the associated enteropathy, with dietitian support
Use dapsone to gain rapid control of itch and blistering while the diet takes effect
Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before starting dapsone and monitor for haemolysis, methaemoglobinaemia and marrow suppression
Substitute an alternative sulphonamide such as sulfapyridine or sulfasalazine when dapsone is not tolerated
Screen for and manage associated conditions including coeliac enteropathy, autoimmune thyroid disease and nutritional deficiencies, in collaboration with gastroenterology
Provide long-term follow-up, tapering medication as the diet controls disease, and note that dietary adherence lowers the associated lymphoma risk
